What would often be a safe distance from 
the teeming predators below the canopy, 
sleeping doves rest amongst the top flowering 
branches of an ironwoood tree. Peacefully 
nestled next to each other as they pair for 
life, they cling to the branches unaware of 
the ynill hatchling looking to practice its aim
Aristo Doves
Height - 4 in.
Ynnil Hatchling
Length - 2 ft. 3 in.
Newly hatched and incessantly squawking, aphistus chicks would not survive a moment in the Wealdwoods had it not been for the 
protective adult kin that keep guard over them night and day. Requiring a steady supply of food to fuel their rapidly growing bodies, 
the chicks are quick to call for their mother the moment she leaves their sight.
By far one of the rarest sights in the Wealdwoods, the timid shaevrynn kitten spends the better part of its fi rst year of life sleeping 
throughout the day and only venturing out under the cover at night. Th e litter of three to four stay close to their mother, learning to 
swim, to hunt and to stay perfectly still when there is any sign of danger. Only the most wary and vigilant survive the woods.
Raised in a close knit familial group, it is rare to fi nd a calitross fledgling alone, clinging to the feathered back of its parents they 
huddle in close against the cold as their kin climb across the upper canopy and way from the dangerous predators that tread below. 
When confronted with danger, the young bird will react with a screeching chirp, to both stun the potential predator and call for aid.
Th e moment the green little lizards hatch from their egg cluster they venture upwards into the canopy. Instinctively sticking close 
together to learn to hunt and survive as a unit, only once they grow too large to traverse the light twigs and branches of the generally 
safer upper treetops do they begin to separate and hunt alone.
